arXiv:cond-mat/0507383v1 [cond-mat.mes-hall] 15 Jul 2005

Theory of Umklapp-assisted recombination of bound excitons in Si:P

Michael N. Leuenberger and L. J. Sham Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We present the calculations for the oscillator strength of the recombination of excitons bound to phosphorous donors in silicon. We show that the direct recombination of the bound exciton cannot account for the experimentally measured oscillator strength of the no-phonon line. Instead, the recombination process is assisted by an umklapp process of the donor electron state. We make use of the empirical pseudopotential method to evaluate the Umklapp-assisted recombination matrix element in second-order perturbation theory. Our result is in excellent agreement with the experiment. We also present two methods to improve the optical resolution of the optical detection of the spin state of a single nucleus in silicon.

I Introduction

Proposals on quantum computing in semiconductors have recently attracted a great deal of attention.[1, 2] The main idea is to use the electron spin of quantum dots in semiconductors[3] or the nuclear spin of shallow donors in silicon[4] as a qubit for quantum information processing. A complete quantum computation consists of, besides the single- and two-qubit operations, the initialization and the readout of the qubits. While the initialization and the readout of the electron spin in quantum dots have been successfully demonstrated experimentally,[5, 6] it remains an experimental challenge to read out the nuclear spin of a donor electron in silicon.

It has recently been proposed that the photoluminescence of excitons bound to phosphorous donors can be used to detect the spin state of a single donor nucleus in silicon.[7] This scheme for optical readout could render the recent quantum computing proposal using conditional NMR and ESR pulses feasible.[9, 10] Although experiments have shown that the recombination of the bound exciton follows strong optical selection rules,[11] it has been unclear what physical process is responsible for the no-phonon line of the optical recombination of the bound exciton. In contrast to the phonon-assisted recombination, the no-phonon line represents the recombination process without phonon assistance. A shell model that accounts for the selection rules has been proposed in Ref. 12. The shell model has been later improved in Ref. 13, 14 by a Hartree-Fock calculation that takes the multivalley character of indirect bandgap semiconductors into account and therefore is in good agreement with the measured fine-structure excitation spectrum of the bound exciton complex.[15] The Hartree-Fock calculation fails to predict binding energies. This problem was overcome by a density-functional calculation that takes the correlation energy into account.[16] However, neither model gives a satisfactory physical description of the recombination process for the no-phonon line and thus is unable to quantitatively reproduce the measured oscillator strength fexpf_{\rm exp} in Ref. 17. Our calculations show that the probability for direct recombination of the bound exciton is negligibly small. Here we present a physical model of the recombination process that accurately reproduces the oscillator strength fexpf_{\rm exp} of the no-phonon line. In our model the recombination of the exciton is assisted by the Umklapp-process of the donor electron. In Sec. II we give a detailed description of our model, where we introduce the Coulomb scattering of the bound and the donor electron. For the evaluation of the recombination matrix element, we make use of the empirical pseudopotential method[18, 19, 20] to calculate the bandstructure of silicon with 137 reciprocal lattice vectors at 100 points inside the first Brillouin zone in X direction. This technique is applied to our model in Sec. III. Then we use the resulting Bloch states to calculate the oscillator strength of the Umklapp-assisted recombination in second-order perturbation theory, which is shown in Sec. IV. In Sec. V we present two methods based on optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) to improve the resolution of the readout of a nuclear spin of a donor electron in silicon.

II Physical model

Our physical model of the Umklapp-assisted recombination is shown in Fig. 1. First the bound electron with wavevector 𝐤B{\bf k}_{\rm B} is scattered via the Coulomb potential

VC=q2​e−r​ξl2+2​ξt24​π​ϵ​rV_{\rm C}=\frac{q^{2}e^{-r\sqrt{\xi_{l}^{2}+2\xi_{t}^{2}}}}{4\pi\epsilon r} (1)

The transverse mass in silicon is mt=0.1905​mem_{t}=0.1905m_{e}. After the Umklapp process the bound electron with wavevector 𝐤B′{\bf k}_{\rm B}^{\prime} recombines with the bound hole with wavevector 𝐤h′=𝐤B′{\bf k}_{\rm h}^{\prime}={\bf k}_{\rm B}^{\prime} via the electron-photon interaction

ℋ=∑ipi22​mi∗+VC+Vr,{\cal H}=\sum_{i}\frac{p_{i}^{2}}{2m_{i}^{*}}+V_{\rm C}+V_{\rm r}, (3)

where the first term is the kinetic energy of the bound electron, the donor electron, and the bound hole with the effective masses mi∗m_{i}^{*}, which takes the lattice potential via the empirical pseudopotential method into account (see App. B).

The transition amplitude of the Umklapp-assisted recombination is given by

III Bandstructure of silicon

We choose the empirical pseudopotential method to calculate the bandstructure of silicon.[18, 19, 20] A brief review of this method is given in App. B. We need to solve the Schrödinger equation for the pseudowavefunction, i.e.,

ℏ2​(𝐤+𝐆)22​me​u𝐆+∑𝐆′V0​(|𝐆−𝐆′|)​u𝐆′=E​u𝐆.\frac{\hbar^{2}({\bf k}+{\bf G})^{2}}{2m_{e}}u_{\bf G}+\sum_{{\bf G}^{\prime}}V_{0}(|{\bf G}-{\bf G}^{\prime}|)u_{{\bf G}^{\prime}}=Eu_{\bf G}. (12)

We diagonalize it using the 137 𝐆{\bf G}-vectors shown in Tab. 1 and the form factors VS​(G=3)=−3.049V_{S}(G=\sqrt{3})=-3.049 eV, VS​(G=8)=0.750V_{S}(G=\sqrt{8})=0.750 eV, and VS​(G=11)=0.985V_{S}(G=\sqrt{11})=0.985 eV.

We calculate the bandstructure of silicon for 100 points in 𝐤{\bf k}-space in the direction of the X point. The bandstructure is shown in Fig. 3. For our Umklapp-assisted recombination the following symmetries are important: the conduction (valence) band at the Γ\Gamma point has the symmetry Γ25′\Gamma_{25^{\prime}} (Γ15\Gamma_{15}), which transforms as {y​z,x​z,x​y}\{yz,xz,xy\} ({x,y,z}\{x,y,z\}). The conduction band at the X point has the symmetry Δ1\Delta_{1}, which transforms as {z}\{z\}. So the initial bound electron state before the recombination has the symmetry Δ1\Delta_{1} and the hole has the symmetry Γ15\Gamma_{15}. Since the spin-orbit splitting at the Γ\Gamma point is Δso=0.044\Delta_{\rm so}=0.044 eV (see Ref. 26), the heavy-hole states including spin are represented by

|J=32;M=32⟩\displaystyle\left|J=\frac{3}{2};M=\frac{3}{2}\right> =\displaystyle= 12(|yz⟩+i|xz⟩)|↑⟩,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\left|yz\right>+i\left|xz\right>\right)\left|\uparrow\right>,
|J=32;M=12⟩\displaystyle\left|J=\frac{3}{2};M=\frac{1}{2}\right> =\displaystyle= 23|xy↑⟩−16|(y+ix)z↓⟩,\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left|xy\uparrow\right>-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left|(y+ix)z\downarrow\right>,
|J=32;M=−12⟩\displaystyle\left|J=\frac{3}{2};M=-\frac{1}{2}\right> =\displaystyle= 23|xy↓⟩+16|(y−ix)z↑⟩,\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left|xy\downarrow\right>+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left|(y-ix)z\uparrow\right>,
|J=32;M=−32⟩\displaystyle\left|J=\frac{3}{2};M=-\frac{3}{2}\right> =\displaystyle= 12(|yz⟩−i|xz⟩)|↓⟩.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\left|yz\right>-i\left|xz\right>\right)\left|\downarrow\right>. (13)

That is the origin of the selection rules found experimentally in Ref. 11.

IV Oscillator strength

In textbooks such as Ref. 27 the oscillator strength is defined as

f=2m​En​i|⟨n|p|i⟩|2,f=\frac{2}{mE_{ni}}\left|\left<n\right|p\left|i\right>\right|^{2}, (14)

where En​iE_{ni} is the energy difference between the initial |i⟩\left|i\right> and the final state |n⟩\left|n\right>. For our Umklapp-assisted recombination the oscillator strength is thus given by

ftot=2mopt​Egap​|ghh​gs​Mtotqmt​A⊥|2,f_{\rm tot}=\frac{2}{m_{\rm opt}E_{\rm gap}}\left|\frac{g_{\rm hh}g_{s}M_{\rm tot}}{\frac{q}{m_{t}}A_{\bot}}\right|^{2}, (15)

where Egap=1.1E_{\rm gap}=1.1 eV is the indirect bandgap energy, mopt=3/(1/ml+2/mt)m_{\rm opt}=3/(1/m_{l}+2/m_{t}) is the effective mass of the electron that ensures the sum rule ∑nfn​i=1\sum_{n}f_{ni}=1,[28] ghh=2g_{\rm hh}=2 is the degeneracy of the heavy-hole band and gs=2g_{s}=2 is the spin degeneracy. We calculate first numerically the Coulomb scattering amplitude MC​(ku)M_{C}(k_{u}), which is shown in Fig. 2. Then we calculate numerically the recombination amplitude Mr​(ku)M_{r}(k_{u}), which is shown in Fig. 4. In Fig. 5 we plot the Umklapp-assisted recombination amplitude M⁡(ku)M(k_{u}). Inserting MC​(ku)M_{C}(k_{u}) and Mr​(ku)M_{r}(k_{u}) into Eq. (4) and integrating over kuk_{u} yields

ftot=10.1×10−6,f_{\rm tot}=10.1\times 10^{-6}, (16)

which is in excellent agreement with the oscillator strength fexp=7.1×10−6f_{\rm exp}=7.1\times 10^{-6} of the recombination of an exciton bound to a phosphorous donor in silicon reported in Ref. 17. For comparison, the direct recombination of the bound electron with the bound hole over the indirect bandgap has an oscillator strength of fdirect=4×10−33f_{\rm direct}=4\times 10^{-33}.

V Optical readout

In this section we show two methods that can be used to improve the optical resolution of the optical detection of the spin state of a single nucleus in silicon (see Ref. 7):

  • •

    The first method is inspired by the optically detected magnetic resonance technique (ODMR)[8], where the induced ESR Rabi oscillation alters the lifetime of the bound exciton and is thus optically detectable. Since the transition from the bound hole state MJ=−3/2M_{J}=-3/2 to MS=+1/2M_{S}=+1/2 is forbidden, mixing the spin states in an equal superposition of MS=+1/2M_{S}=+1/2 and MS=−1/2M_{S}=-1/2 leads to a doubling of the lifetime of the bound exciton.

  • •

    The second method makes use of a strong ESR field that renormalizes the spin levels in such a way that the hyperfine and Zeeman splitting of the nuclear spin is increased. As in the first method, the photons of the ESR field dress the spin states of the donor electron.

The Hamiltonian for the electron-nucleus system is

ℋs=ge​μB​𝐇⋅𝐒−gn​μn​𝐇⋅𝐈+A​𝐒⋅𝐈{\cal H}_{s}=g_{e}\mu_{B}{\bf H}\cdot{\bf S}-g_{n}\mu_{n}{\bf H}\cdot{\bf I}+A{\bf S}\cdot{\bf I} (17)

in the generalized rotating frame. If we choose the basis {|↑e↑n⟩,|↑e↓n⟩,|↓e↑n⟩,|↓e↓n⟩}\{\left|\uparrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}\right>,\left|\uparrow_{e}\downarrow_{n}\right>,\left|\downarrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}\right>,\left|\downarrow_{e}\downarrow_{n}\right>\}, the Hamiltonian reads

ℋs=[ge​μB2​Hz−gn​μn2​Hz+A4−gn​μn2​Hxge​μB2​Hx0−gn​μn2​Hxge​μB2​Hz+gn​μn2​Hz−A4−A2ge​μB2​Hxge​μB2​Hx−A2−ge​μB2​Hz−gn​μn2​Hz−A4−gn​μn2​Hx0ge​μB2​Hx−gn​μn2​Hx−ge​μB2​Hz+gn​μn2​Hz+A4].{\cal H}_{\rm s}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{A}{4}&-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{x}&\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{x}&0\\ -\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{x}&\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{A}{4}&-\frac{A}{2}&\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{x}\\ \frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{x}&-\frac{A}{2}&-\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{A}{4}&-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{x}\\ 0&\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{x}&-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{x}&-\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{A}{4}\end{array}\right]. (18)

The energy levels of the electron and nuclear spin are shown in Fig. 6.

Typical external magnetic fields used in experiments are Hz=3.0,5.0H_{z}=3.0,5.0, and 7.07.0 T. In a field of Hz=3.0H_{z}=3.0 T the Zeeman splittings of the electron and nuclear spin are ge​μB​Hz=0.35g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{z}=0.35 meV and gn​μn​Hz=0.21g_{n}\mu_{n}H_{z}=0.21 μ\mueV, respectively. The hyperfine splitting is A=0.50A=0.50 μ\mueV. Thus the splitting between |↑e↑n⟩\left|\uparrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}\right> and |↑e↓n⟩\left|\uparrow_{e}\downarrow_{n}\right> is Δ↑e=E↑e↑n−E↑e↓n=A/2−gnμnHz=0.03\Delta_{\uparrow_{e}}=E_{\uparrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}}-E_{\uparrow_{e}\downarrow_{n}}=A/2-g_{n}\mu_{n}H_{z}=0.03 μ\mueV, whereas the splitting between |↓e↑n⟩\left|\downarrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}\right> and |↓e↓n⟩\left|\downarrow_{e}\downarrow_{n}\right> is Δ↓e=E↓e↓n−E↓e↑n=A/2+gnμnHz=0.46\Delta_{\downarrow_{e}}=E_{\downarrow_{e}\downarrow_{n}}-E_{\downarrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}}=A/2+g_{n}\mu_{n}H_{z}=0.46 μ\mueV. The hyperfine and Zeeman splittings for Hz=3.0,5.0H_{z}=3.0,5.0, and 7.07.0 T are shown in Tab. 2.

where tan2θ=−Ω/(ω−ω0)\tan 2\theta=-\Omega/\left(\omega-\omega_{0}\right), 0≤2​θ<π0\leq 2\theta<\pi. The eigenenergies are

E1/2=(N+12)​ℏ​ω±ℏ​(ω−ω02)2+(Ω2)2.E_{1/2}=\left(N+\frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar\omega\pm\hbar\sqrt{\left(\frac{\omega-\omega_{0}}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\Omega}{2}\right)^{2}}. (28)

Let us tune the oscillating transverse microwave field to the transition between |↑e↑n⟩\left|\uparrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}\right> and |↓e↑n⟩\left|\downarrow_{e}\uparrow_{n}\right>. Then the eigenstates are

|χ↑n1⟩\displaystyle\left|\chi_{\uparrow_{n}1}\right> =\displaystyle= (|ϕ↓e⟩+|ϕ↑e⟩)|↑n⟩/2,\displaystyle\left(\left|\phi_{\downarrow_{e}}\right>+\left|\phi_{\uparrow_{e}}\right>\right)\left|\uparrow_{n}\right>/\sqrt{2},
|χ↓n1⟩\displaystyle\left|\chi_{\downarrow_{n}1}\right> =\displaystyle= (sinθ|ϕ↓e⟩+cosθ|ϕ↑e⟩)|↓n⟩/2,\displaystyle\left(\sin\theta\left|\phi_{\downarrow_{e}}\right>+\cos\theta\left|\phi_{\uparrow_{e}}\right>\right)\left|\downarrow_{n}\right>/\sqrt{2},
|χ↓n2⟩\displaystyle\left|\chi_{\downarrow_{n}2}\right> =\displaystyle= (cosθ|ϕ↓e⟩−sinθ|ϕ↑e⟩)|↓n⟩/2,\displaystyle\left(\cos\theta\left|\phi_{\downarrow_{e}}\right>-\sin\theta\left|\phi_{\uparrow_{e}}\right>\right)\left|\downarrow_{n}\right>/\sqrt{2},
|χ↑n2⟩\displaystyle\left|\chi_{\uparrow_{n}2}\right> =\displaystyle= (|ϕ↓e⟩−|ϕ↑e⟩)|↑n⟩/2,\displaystyle\left(\left|\phi_{\downarrow_{e}}\right>-\left|\phi_{\uparrow_{e}}\right>\right)\left|\uparrow_{n}\right>/\sqrt{2}, (29)

where tan2θ=−12geμBHx/A\tan 2\theta=-\frac{1}{2}g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}/A. The eigenenergies of the electron-nucleus system are

E↑n1\displaystyle E_{\uparrow_{n}1} =\displaystyle= −ge​μB2​Hz−gn​μn2​Hz−A4−ge​μB​Hx2,\displaystyle-\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{A}{4}-\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}}{2},
E↓n1\displaystyle E_{\downarrow_{n}1} =\displaystyle= −ge​μB2​Hz+gn​μn2​Hz+(A4)2+(ge​μB​Hx2)2,\displaystyle-\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}+\sqrt{\left(\frac{A}{4}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}}{2}\right)^{2}},
E↓n2\displaystyle E_{\downarrow_{n}2} =\displaystyle= ge​μB2​Hz+gn​μn2​Hz−(A4)2+(ge​μB​Hx2)2,\displaystyle\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}-\sqrt{\left(\frac{A}{4}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}}{2}\right)^{2}},
E↑n2\displaystyle E_{\uparrow_{n}2} =\displaystyle= ge​μB2​Hz−gn​μn2​Hz+A4+ge​μB​Hx2.\displaystyle\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}}{2}H_{z}-\frac{g_{n}\mu_{n}}{2}H_{z}+\frac{A}{4}+\frac{g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}}{2}. (30)

The oscillator strength for the exciton recombination in Si:P is f=7.1×10−6f=7.1\times 10^{-6} (see Ref. 17). The binding energy of the exciton to the phosophorus donor is Ebinding=4.7E_{\rm binding}=4.7 meV. The recombination rate is about w=400w=400 s-1. This leads to an interaction energy of

Eint=ℏ​w​Γ=12​neV,E_{\rm int}=\sqrt{\hbar w\Gamma}=12\,{\rm neV}, (31)

where Γ=100\Gamma=100 μ\mueV is the linewidth of the recombination.

If the electron-photon interaction energy EintE_{\rm int} is much weaker than the microwave coupling energy ge​μB​Hxg_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}, the states |χ↑n1⟩\left|\chi_{\uparrow_{n}1}\right>, |χ↓n1⟩\left|\chi_{\downarrow_{n}1}\right>, |χ↓n2⟩\left|\chi_{\downarrow_{n}2}\right>, and |χ↑n2⟩\left|\chi_{\uparrow_{n}2}\right> are good eigenstates. Then the ODMR method works, because the final state of the radiative recombination is given by |χ↑n1⟩\left|\chi_{\uparrow_{n}1}\right>, which doubles the lifetime of the bound exciton. The transverse microwave field should have a strength of at least Hx=1.0H_{x}=1.0 G, leading to a microwave coupling energy of ge​μB​Hx=10.0g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}=10.0 neV.

In addition, it can be seen from Eq. (30) that the hyperfine splittings are increased, which effectively increases the optical resolution. In order to obtain at least a 10% increase of the hyperfine+Zeeman splitting of the two lowest energy levels, the oscillating transverse magnetic field must have a strength of 10.010.0 G, which yields the transverse Zeeman splittings of the electron and nuclear spin of ge​μB​Hx=0.12g_{e}\mu_{B}H_{x}=0.12 μ\mueV and gn​μn​Hx=0.07g_{n}\mu_{n}H_{x}=0.07 neV, respectively. For a longitudinal magnetic field of Hz=3.0H_{z}=3.0 T, the shifted hyperfine splitting is Δ2=E↑n2−E↓n2=0.10\Delta_{2}=E_{\uparrow_{n}2}-E_{\downarrow_{n}2}=0.10 μ\mueV, whereas Δ1=E↓n1−E↑n1=0.53\Delta_{1}=E_{\downarrow_{n}1}-E_{\uparrow_{n}1}=0.53 μ\mueV. The shifted hyperfine and Zeeman splittings for Hz=3.0,5.0H_{z}=3.0,5.0, and 7.07.0 T are shown in Tab. 3.

The frequency-resolved photon detection has the advantage that a single photon detection is sufficient for determining the spin of the nucleus, whereas the ODMR measurement needs to be done in an ensemble in order to determine the radiative recombination time. Maybe the hyperfine+Zeeman splitting of Δ↓e=A/2+gnμnHz=0.75\Delta_{\downarrow_{e}}=A/2+g_{n}\mu_{n}H_{z}=0.75 μ\mueV in a Hz=7.0H_{z}=7.0 T field is already sufficient for frequency-resolved photon detection.

VI Conclusion

We calculated the oscillator strength of recombination of an exciton bound to a donor electron in silicon. We showed that the Umklapp-assisted recombination, consisting of a scattering between the bound electron and the donor electron and the recombination of the unbound scattered electron, gives the main contribution. The calculation of the Umklapp-assisted recombination was done in second-order perturbation theory. We made use of the empirical pseudopotential method to find the Bloch wavefunctions of silicon. The calculated oscillator strength is in excellent agreement with the experiment. We gave also two methods to improve the resolution of the detection of a nuclear spin of a donor electron in silicon.

Appendix B Empirical Pseudopotential Method

We give here a brief review of the empirical pseudopotential method. At each lattice site there is an atom with a nucleus, core electrons, and valence electrons. The attractive nuclear potential VnV_{\rm n} is large and varies strongly throughout the lattice. The main observation is that VnV_{\rm n} is almost canceled by the repulsive potential VrepV_{\rm rep} produced by the core electrons. So we need to consider only the valence electrons moving in a net weak one-electron potential VpV_{\rm p}, which is called the pseudopotential.

The full Bloch wavefunctions can be expressed as

Φ=ϕ+∑tαt​φt.\Phi=\phi+\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}\varphi_{t}. (44)

Φ\Phi must be orthogonal to the core wave functions φt\varphi_{t}, i.e. ⟨φt|Φ⟩=0\left<\varphi_{t}|\Phi\right>=0, which yields

αt=−⟨φt|ϕ⟩.\alpha_{t}=-\left<\varphi_{t}|\phi\right>. (45)

Then applying the Hamiltonian ℋn=p2/2​me+Vn{\cal H}_{\rm n}=p^{2}/2m_{e}+V_{\rm n} to Φ\Phi leads to the Schrödinger equation

(p22​me+Vn+Vrep)​ϕ=E​ϕ,\left(\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{e}}+V_{\rm n}+V_{\rm rep}\right)\phi=E\phi, (46)

where the short-range non-Hermitian repulsive potential is given by

Vrep​ϕ=∑t(E−Et)​φt​⟨φt|ϕ⟩,V_{\rm rep}\phi=\sum_{t}\left(E-E_{t}\right)\varphi_{t}\left<\varphi_{t}|\phi\right>, (47)

with EE being the full energy eigenvalue of Φ\Phi. ϕ\phi is called the pseudowavefunction. Since the crystal potential is periodic, the pseudopotential Vp=Vn+VrepV_{\rm p}=V_{\rm n}+V_{\rm rep} and can be expanded in a Fourier series over the reciprocal lattice vectors 𝐆{\bf G}, i.e.

Vp=∑𝐆V~0​(𝐆)​ei​𝐆⋅𝐫,V_{\rm p}=\sum_{\bf G}\tilde{V}_{0}({\bf G})e^{i{\bf G}\cdot{\bf r}}, (48)

where

V~0(𝐆)=1L3∫d3rV0(𝐫)e−i𝐆⋅𝐫.\tilde{V}_{0}({\bf G})=\frac{1}{L^{3}}\int d^{3}rV_{0}({\bf r})e^{-i{\bf G}\cdot{\bf r}}. (49)

For zincblende and diamond lattices usually a two-atom basis is chosen, such that

V0​(𝐫)=Vcation​(𝐫−τ)+Vanion​(𝐫+τ),V_{0}({\bf r})=V_{\rm cation}({\bf r}-\tau)+V_{\rm anion}({\bf r}+\tau), (50)

where 𝝉=(1,1,1)​d/8\mbox{\boldmath$\tau$}=(1,1,1)d/8. Then the Fourier potential reads

V~0(𝐆)=ei​𝐆⋅𝝉V~cation(𝐆)+e−i𝐆⋅𝝉V~anion(𝐆).\tilde{V}_{0}({\bf G})=e^{i{\bf G}\cdot\mbox{\boldmath$\tau$}}\tilde{V}_{\rm cation}({\bf G})+e^{-i{\bf G}\cdot\mbox{\boldmath$\tau$}}\tilde{V}_{\rm anion}({\bf G}). (51)

The Fourier coefficients can be rewritten in terms of the symmetric and antisymmetric form factors V~S=V~cation+V~anion\tilde{V}_{S}=\tilde{V}_{\rm cation}+\tilde{V}_{\rm anion} and V~A=V~cation−V~anion\tilde{V}_{A}=\tilde{V}_{\rm cation}-\tilde{V}_{\rm anion}. Thus

V~0​(𝐆)=cos⁡(𝐆⋅𝝉)​V~S​(𝐆)+i​sin⁡(𝐆⋅𝝉)​V~A​(𝐆),\tilde{V}_{0}({\bf G})=\cos({\bf G}\cdot\mbox{\boldmath$\tau$})\tilde{V}_{S}({\bf G})+i\sin({\bf G}\cdot\mbox{\boldmath$\tau$})\tilde{V}_{A}({\bf G}), (52)

where the prefactors of the form factors are the structure factors. Since silicon has a diamond lattice, V~A​(𝐆)=0\tilde{V}_{A}({\bf G})=0.

The pseudowavefunction can also be expanded in a Fourier series, i.e.

ϕ⁡(𝐫)=ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​u​(𝐫)=ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​∑𝐆u𝐆​ei​𝐆⋅𝐫.\phi({\bf r})=e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}u({\bf r})=e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}\sum_{\bf G}u_{\bf G}e^{i{\bf G}\cdot{\bf r}}. (53)

Inserting the pseudowavefunction ϕ\phi and the pseudopotential VpV_{\rm p} into Eq. (46) yields

ℏ2​(𝐤+𝐆)22​me​u𝐆+∑𝐆′V0​(|𝐆−𝐆′|)​u𝐆′=E​u𝐆.\frac{\hbar^{2}({\bf k}+{\bf G})^{2}}{2m_{e}}u_{\bf G}+\sum_{{\bf G}^{\prime}}V_{0}(|{\bf G}-{\bf G}^{\prime}|)u_{{\bf G}^{\prime}}=Eu_{\bf G}. (54)

Diagonalization of this Hamiltonian yields an effective mass Hamiltonian, which is the first term on the right side of Eq. (3).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
